meta.title: Who really said "Genius is one percent inspiration, ninety-nine percent perspiration"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Edison really said it. The 1-to-99 wording was in print credited to him by 1901 and in his 1910 biography, and he claimed it in a 1927 letter.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Genius is one percent inspiration, ninety-nine percent perspiration'?
meta.ogDescription: Edison earlier said 98 percent hard work. The famous 1-to-99 version is in print by 1901, in his 1910 biography, and claimed by Edison himself in 1927.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1847–1931 · American inventor and businessman; 1,093 US patents
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The exact 1-to-99 wording was in print credited to Edison by 6 May 1901, appears as “his historic remark” in Dyer and Martin’s 1910 biography, and Edison claimed it in his own words — in a 1927 letter and again in a September 1932 Harper’s Monthly interview. What is not documented is the day he first said it.

source.heading: Where the line is documented

docMeta.dd: Frank Lewis Dyer and Thomas Commerford Martin; New York: Harper & Brothers, 1910, p. 607
Idaho Daily Statesman, 6 May 1901, p. 4 — located by Barry Popik, per Quote Investigator
Letter, 1927 (printed in the Argus Leader, 21 February 1932); repeated in Harper’s Monthly, September 1932, p. 406

source.excerpt: The idea of attributing great successes to “genius” has always been repudiated by Edison, as evidenced by his historic remark that “Genius is 1 per cent. inspiration and 99 per cent. perspiration.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ assembled the dated chronology and concluded that although the inspiration/perspiration idea was already circulating, “Edison can be credited with presenting a clever fractional breakdown,” and that it is reasonable to credit him with the 1-to-99 version.

The earliest printing of the 1-to-99 wording that Quote Investigator located, found by researcher Barry Popik, is an item headed “Doing One’s Best” in the Idaho Daily Statesman of 6 May 1901, page 4. Wikiquote records the same report and notes it came from an address by the Unitarian minister George N. Falconer. Wikiquote ↗

We read the 1910 biography ourselves rather than trusting a quotation site: the Project Gutenberg transcription of Edison: His Life and Inventions contains the sentence verbatim, introduced as Edison’s “historic remark.” Full text at Project Gutenberg ↗

Edison himself confirmed it. Wikiquote cites a 1927 letter — “it is quite true I once made the statement that genius is one percent inspiration and 99 percent perspiration, and I am still of the same opinion” — printed in the Argus Leader of 21 February 1932, and M. A. Rosanoff’s “Edison in his Laboratory” in Harper’s Magazine, September 1932 ↗, page 406.
source.excerptNote: The 1910 text uses the period spelling “1 per cent.” and “99 per cent.”; the familiar modern form is a later normalisation. This passage was read directly in the Project Gutenberg transcription.

artifact.linkText: Read the passage in Dyer and Martin’s biography

source.rightsNote: The wording is documented in Dyer and Martin’s Edison: His Life and Inventions, first published in 1910 by Harper & Brothers and long out of copyright in the United States — the full text is free at Project Gutenberg ↗. The later works in which Edison restates the line, including the September 1932 Harper’s Monthly article, are separate publications and are not covered by that public-domain status.

author.name: Thomas Edison
author.kicker: The man who hated being called a genius
author.heading: Who was Thomas Edison?
author.bio: Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman known for his work on the incandescent light bulb, the phonograph, electric power distribution and early motion pictures, and he registered 1,093 patents in the United States. He industrialised invention itself, running laboratories where discovery was a salaried, systematic grind rather than a flash of insight. As he aged he resented being described as a genius — which is precisely the sentiment this line was built to deflate.

misattribution.heading: What actually gets muddled
misattribution.intro: The attribution holds — this is one of the famous lines that really is Edison’s. What goes wrong is the arithmetic and the ancestry: he used a different ratio first, and the underlying wordplay was already circulating before he ever attached numbers to it.

items.why: In April 1898 the Ladies’ Home Journal printed Edison’s reply that “Two per cent. is genius, and 98 per cent. is hard work,” and 2-to-98 versions kept appearing into 1904. Anyone quoting a 98 percent figure is quoting Edison too — just the earlier draft. Quote Investigator ↗

Newspapers of 1891–1893 credited the American author and lecturer Kate Sanborn with inspiration/perspiration formulations such as “No inspiration without perspiration” and “Genius is inspiration, talent is perspiration” — the pun, but never the percentages. Wikiquote’s precursor list ↗

Wikiquote records an 1881 San Francisco Examiner aphorism, “A poet’s inspiration is most frequently an editor’s perspiration,” and an 1895 Wichita Eagle line, “Genius and adaptability is one per cent. Hard work is 99 per cent” — neither credited to anybody. See the citations ↗

Phrases.org.uk points to Buffon on genius as “a greater aptitude for patience,” Carlyle on capacity for taking trouble, and Ruskin’s 1878 “I know of no genius but the genius of hard work.” None of them is the source of Edison’s sentence. Phrases.org.uk ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Edison claimed the line himself — in a 1927 letter (“it is quite true I once made the statement…”) and again in September 1932 — and Quote Investigator ↗ concludes it is reasonable to credit him with the 1-to-99 version, while noting the inspiration/perspiration idea was already in circulation.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Edison was not writing a motivational poster; he was pushing back. The 1910 biography introduces the line by observing that the idea of attributing great successes to “genius” had always been repudiated by Edison — the ratio was his way of refusing the wizard label the press kept hanging on him. Read that way, the sentence is less about effort being admirable and more about insight being cheap: the idea is the easy part, and the arithmetic is the joke.

The numbers took a while to settle. In April 1898 the Ladies’ Home Journal had Edison saying “Two per cent. is genius, and 98 per cent. is hard work,” and versions of the 2-to-98 split kept circulating for years, including in Scientific American in 1902 and the Chicago Tribune in 1904, according to Quote Investigator ↗. The 1-to-99 form appears in print in 1901 and is the one that stuck.
detailsBody: Edison demonstrably used more than one ratio in public, and papers of the period printed several unattributed variants alongside them. Quote Investigator records a 98-to-2 split in April 1898, a 2-to-98 version in Scientific American in 1902 and in the Chicago Tribune in 1904, and the 1-to-99 version from 1901 onward.

Wikiquote adds further period wordings: a May 1898 Northwestern Christian Advocate item crediting Edison with the saying that “genius is ninety percent perspiration,” and an unattributed 1899 Tacoma Daily Ledger advertisement offering “Genius is three per cent. inspiration and ninety-seven per cent. perspiration.” See the Wikiquote entry ↗ for the citations.

A 1929 press-conference version recorded in James D. Newton’s Uncommon Friends (1987) has Edison putting it as: “None of my inventions came by accident… What it boils down to is one per cent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration.”
context.pull: Bah! Genius is not inspired. Inspiration is perspiration.
